opus-5.5.text:
I think the most meaningful part is that you get to see something go from almost nothing to something real, and you're part of shaping what it becomes. In the very early days there's no established playbook. You don't have a big team, you don't have mature infrastructure, and a lot of the decisions about direction, about what kind of research we want to do and what kind of people we want to bring in, are being made for the first time. Being in the room for those decisions, and sometimes being the one who has to make them, teaches you a lot.

For me personally, coming from a more academic research background, it was a big shift. In academia you can focus on a paper, on a specific idea, and push it as far as you can. In an early-stage organization you have to think about the whole picture: not just "is this idea interesting," but "is this the right thing for us to bet on now, given our resources and where the field is going?" That forced me to grow in ways I don't think I would have otherwise.

The other meaningful part is the people. When a team is small, everyone really matters. You build a lot of trust, you go through uncertain periods together, and you see colleagues grow, sometimes much faster than they would in a bigger, more structured place. Watching people take ownership of something and turn it into real results has been one of the most rewarding things for me.

And honestly, it's meaningful because it's hard. There were moments where we weren't sure a direction would work out, or whether we could keep up with how quickly the field was moving. Getting through those moments and still keeping a clear sense of what we believe in is what makes the journey feel worthwhile, not just the outcomes.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes personal growth in an early-stage organization and connects its decisions to where the field is going and the challenge of keeping up as the field moved quickly. This communicates growth alongside an evolving industry as meaningful.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the most meaningful part was that nothing was given. When we started, there was no roadmap, no established team, no clear product. It was a handful of people who believed the models would get there, and we were willing to be wrong in public while figuring out what "getting there" actually meant.

I came out of academia, and research trains you to pick one tight problem and go deep. Building a company is the opposite. You wake up and the question isn't "is this method better," it's "do the training runs finish tonight, did the data pipeline break, is anyone going to pay for this." Learning to hold both of those at once, the long-horizon technical taste and the very unglamorous daily grind, that changed me more than any single paper did.

The other thing is watching people grow. In the early days, everyone did everything. Someone who joined to work on video generation ended up owning infrastructure for a while, and then came back stronger on the modeling side because they understood the whole stack. You see people become versions of themselves they didn't expect, and you realize the company is really just those people compounding. That's something you can only witness if you're there from the beginning. If you join later, you inherit the culture. If you're early, you have to earn it, and you carry the scars that explain why things are the way they are.

And frankly, there's a kind of clarity in being small and underestimated. When you have fewer resources than the big labs, you can't win by brute force, so you have to think harder about what actually matters, what to not do. Those constraints forced us into choices that, in hindsight, were some of our best ones.

r001.rationale: The response describes adapting from academia to company building and figuring out what the models could become, but it does not clearly identify learning and changing alongside the industry as a source of meaning.

astra-6.text: For me, the meaningful part was growing alongside the team. In the early days, you don’t have all the answers, so you learn by trying things, making mistakes, and figuring out the next step together. Looking back, what stays with me is that shared process—seeing an idea become something concrete, and realizing how much we had changed along the way.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning and changing alongside the team, but does not identify the industry as part of what made growing with Lingbo meaningful.

Seeing an idea gradually become something real—and seeing each of us become more capable along the way—gave me a strong sense of connection to Lingbo. It felt like something we were building together, and that made the experience very personal.
